questions.prompt: What four questions does an executive audience actually need answered?
options: Which tools were used, by whom, when, and how
Is it over, what was taken, what must we disclose and by when, and what does fixing it cost versus not fixing it
Which ATT&CK techniques applied and their IDs
How many hosts, how many users, how many alerts, how many hours
questions.explanation: Everything else is supporting detail. An executive summary that opens with the intrusion vector rather than whether it is over has buried the point.

questions.prompt: What does 'no evidence' mean in confidence language, and what does it not mean?
options: It means the event definitely did not occur
It means you looked and found nothing -- which is not the same as establishing that it did not happen
It means the investigation is incomplete
questions.explanation: Conflating absence of evidence with evidence of absence is one of the most consequential reporting errors, particularly where notification decisions depend on it.

questions.prompt: Why should a report explicitly state what could not be determined?
options: Regulators generally treat unprovable scope as worst-case scope, so an explicit statement about expired logs is more defensible -- and often more favourable -- than silence that reads as a claim
To shift responsibility to another team
Because incomplete reports cannot be published
questions.explanation: Documenting gaps also directs the instrumentation improvements that prevent the same limitation recurring.

questions.prompt: Why does stating a hypothesis as fact damage an entire report?
options: If the claim later fails, every other finding in the report becomes suspect -- and decisions such as breach notification may have been made on it
Hypotheses cannot be included in reports at all
questions.explanation: Precision in confidence language protects both the decisions built on the report and the credibility of the findings that were correct.
